    • Support and resistance

    Supply and demand zones: the base before a sharp move

    A supply or demand zone is the area price left sharply after pausing there briefly. If price left upward, the zone is marked as demand; if it left downward, as supply. These zones are often fresh areas that have not been tested again yet.

    What is a supply or demand zone?

    Price sometimes pauses in a narrow area for a few candles and then leaves it sharply and in one direction. The narrow area of the pause is called the base. If price left the base upward, the base is marked as a demand zone; if it left downward, as a supply zone.

    The difference from support and resistance is this: support and resistance is an area where price has reacted many times in the past. A supply or demand zone comes from a single sharp departure and is often a fresh zone that has not been tested again yet.

    Directions

    • Demand zone: a base price left with a sharp rise. When price later comes back to it from above, the zone can work as support.
    • Supply zone: a base price left with a sharp drop. When price later comes back to it from below, the zone can work as resistance.

    Before and after the base

    Depending on the move before and after the base, a zone shows up in four forms.

    • Drop · base · rally (DBR): the drop stops and price rallies sharply from the base. A reversal demand zone.
    • Rally · base · rally (RBR): the rise continues after a short pause. A continuation demand zone.
    • Rally · base · drop (RBD): the rise stops and price drops sharply from the base. A reversal supply zone.
    • Drop · base · drop (DBD): the drop continues after a short pause. A continuation supply zone.

    How is it marked?

    Each step gives the demand zone first, then the supply zone.

    1. Find the sharp departure Look for a move in one direction with large-bodied candles; a rise for demand, a drop for supply.
    2. Find the base The few small-bodied candles where price paused right before the departure are marked as the base. Their bodies are clearly smaller than those of the departure candles.
    3. Draw the edges In a demand zone the lower edge is the base's lowest wick and the upper edge its highest point. In a supply zone the upper edge is the base's highest wick and the lower edge its lowest point. The edge price will touch first when it comes back is the proximal edge, the other one the distal edge.
    4. Extend the zone to the right The zone is extended to the right until price comes back. During that time the zone counts as "fresh".

    How it relates to the order block

    An order block is the single-candle form of a supply or demand zone: the last opposite candle of the base, right before the sharp departure. When the base is made of several candles rather than one, the zone is also called a supply or demand cluster.

    A base on a larger timeframe often holds a narrower order block when looked at on a smaller timeframe. The wide zone gives the context, the narrow one the detail.

    What makes a zone stronger

    • The departure is sharp and fast; large-bodied candles, often with an FVG behind them.
    • Price spent little time in the base; a few candles, not a long sideways market.
    • The departure broke structure (BOS or CHoCH).
    • The zone has not been tested yet. Each new test can weaken its effect.
    • The zone is close to an important support or resistance area on a larger timeframe.

    These features make the zone more meaningful; they do not guarantee that price will turn there.

    When price comes back

    When price returns to a zone, one of three pictures usually follows. Each card gives the demand zone first, then the supply zone.

    Reaction

    Price enters the zone through the proximal edge, closes stay inside it and price leaves again; it rises from a demand zone and falls from a supply zone.

    Weak reaction

    Price lingers in the zone and the move away stays short. The zone is no longer "fresh".

    Zone invalidated

    A candle closes beyond the distal edge; below it for a demand zone, above it for a supply zone. The zone is invalidated and can later work in the opposite direction (see breaker block).

    What it shows, what it does not prove

    What it shows

    • Which area price left sharply
    • A fresh zone that can be watched when price comes back
    • That the zone's validity can be measured with a clear closing rule

    What it does not prove

    • That unfilled buy or sell orders are waiting in the zone
    • That price must come back to the zone
    • That price coming back to the zone must turn there

    The MarketLevelMap view

    How it relates to zones

    MarketLevelMap's charts do not draw supply and demand zones separately, but related marks are on the page.

    • The support and resistance zones on the Critical Zones charts are areas where price has reacted again and again. A fresh supply or demand zone close to one of them is more meaningful.
    • The FVG boxes in the Price Action view show the gap a sharp departure left behind. A demand or supply zone is often right at the start of that gap.

    Timeframes

    On small timeframes bases and departures form very often and most zones are short-lived. A zone on a larger timeframe is wider and is watched for longer. A zone is read together with the timeframe it was marked on.

    Often confused with

    • What are support and resistance?Support and resistance is an area where price has reacted many times; a supply or demand zone comes from a single sharp departure and is often untested.
    • Order block (OB): the last opposite candle before a sharp moveAn order block is the single-candle form of the zone; a supply or demand zone also covers a base of several candles.
    • Ranges and consolidationA base is a short pause of a few candles; a range is a phase in which price moves back and forth between two zones for a long time.

    Key points

    • A zone is a short base that price left sharply.
    • Leaving upward gives a demand zone, leaving downward a supply zone.
    • A fresh zone and a sharp departure make the zone more meaningful.
    • A close beyond the distal edge invalidates the zone.
